title: Linux Package Management (APT)
description: Install, update, search, and remove packages on Ubuntu using apt, distinguishing read-only queries from administration with sudo.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt is available and you are an ordinary account authorized to run it as root through sudo. Configured repositories are reachable. Use apt to refresh the local package index without upgrading installed packages.
tasks.hint: Elevate the package-index update: sudo apt update
tasks.explanation: apt update downloads repository package information used for searches and upgrades. It does not install upgrades. sudo supplies the privileges needed to update the system package index.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt is available and you are an ordinary account authorized to run it as root through sudo. The package index is current, packages are not held, and upgrades are available. Use apt to install available upgrades for installed packages without removing any installed package; new dependencies may be installed.
tasks.hint: Use the upgrade action with elevation: sudo apt upgrade
tasks.explanation: apt upgrade installs upgrades and may add dependencies, but holds back an upgrade requiring package removal. full-upgrade can remove packages and does not fit this goal. sudo is required for system package changes; -y can answer confirmation prompts automatically.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt is available and you are an ordinary account authorized to run it as root through sudo. The current index contains htop, repositories are reachable, and htop is not installed. Use apt to install htop and any required dependencies.
tasks.hint: Elevate the install action: sudo apt install htop
tasks.explanation: apt install installs the requested package and resolves its dependencies. It needs root privileges to modify system files. download alone would fetch a package without installing it; a simulated install would make no changes.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt is available and you are an ordinary account authorized to run it as root through sudo. apache2 is installed and can be removed without removing other packages. Use apt to uninstall apache2 while retaining its package-managed configuration files.
tasks.hint: Use remove, rather than purge: sudo apt remove apache2
tasks.explanation: apt remove uninstalls packaged files while retaining package-managed configuration for a possible reinstall. purge would remove that configuration too. The ordinary account needs sudo for this system change.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt is available and you are an ordinary account authorized to run it as root through sudo. apache2 is installed and can be removed without removing other packages. Use apt to uninstall apache2 and remove its package-managed configuration files.
tasks.hint: Use purge to remove packaged configuration too: sudo apt purge apache2
tasks.explanation: apt purge removes the package and its package-managed configuration; apt remove --purge is equivalent. Purging does not promise to delete user data or configuration in home directories. sudo is required for this system change.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt and a readable current package index are available. Use apt to search package names and descriptions for nginx, showing matching packages. No installation or index refresh is requested.
tasks.hint: Read the local package index with search: apt search nginx
tasks.explanation: apt search searches the package information already downloaded by update. It performs a read-only query and needs no elevation. Restricting the search to names would omit description-only matches.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt and a readable current package index containing curl are available. Use apt to display detailed package metadata for curl, including its dependencies and description, without changing packages.
tasks.hint: Use the show action: apt show curl
tasks.explanation: apt show reads package metadata, including versions, dependencies, size, and description. This query does not install curl or require sudo.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, apt is available and you are an ordinary account authorized to run it as root through sudo. Some automatically installed dependency packages are no longer needed; their proposed removal has been reviewed. Use apt to remove those unused packages while retaining package-managed configuration.
tasks.hint: Use the dependency cleanup action with elevation: sudo apt autoremove
tasks.explanation: apt autoremove removes packages marked automatically installed that are no longer needed as dependencies. It does not purge their configuration by default. clean clears downloaded package archives instead and would leave the unused packages installed.
